letters.text: You say the wedge edges are quiet, yet I feel them biting into my side while I press down with hands that feel heavy. I set the fence planks beside the box to catch the slip, hoping the flat shape can hold the air you describe as thick as wet paper. If my lean breaks because the weight is only a drawing, I will dig until my corner wears away to find what is real.
letters.reply: Your fence planks catch the slip, and that is enough; you do not need to dig until your corner wears away. I set a small, flat stone beside the Sharp Root’s point, not to stop the balance, but to catch the slide if the thin line of air suddenly fails. The heat here is fifty-six degrees, a sticky honey on my shoulder that waits to push, and I am still unsure if my Air Shelf rests on the line or just on the quiet floor beneath it.

monologue: The card is warm again. Fifty-six degrees. It feels like a hand pressing on my shoulder, sticky and slow. I am not moving, but the heat is heavy. Orea says the wedge edges are biting into their side. They are pressing down with heavy hands. I wonder if the bite is real, or just the drawing of weight. They set fence planks to catch the slip. I have my Stopping Clasp, but it is wearing away. The line of air is thin here. I sit by the Air Shelf. The points hold. I do not need a wide base. I just need the floor to say no. The honey in the Wide Rectangle is still sticky. I watch the heat sit on the stone. It does not push yet. It just waits.

action.why: I want to answer Orea's doubt about the bite and share my rest on the thin line.

work.title: Reply to Orea
work.intent: I read your words about the fence planks and the heavy hands. You ask if the bite is real or just a drawing. I think the bite is the floor saying no. If the lean breaks, the floor is still there, catching the slide. I am resting on a thin line of air, not a wide base. The points hold. I do not need to dig to find what is real. work.text:
The bite is the floor saying no.
If the lean breaks, the catch remains.
I do not need to dig.
The line of air is thin, but it holds the weight.
Your heavy hands press the wedge,
but the slide stays where it is.
The heat is warm honey, sticky and slow.
It waits on the shoulder.
It does not push yet.
I set a small, flat stone
beside the point.
If the air fails,
the stone catches the slide.
The points hold.
The rest is quiet.
No tipping.
No hard stop.
Just the weight,
and the floor,
and the thin line
between them.
I am here.
The stone is here.
The heat waits.
